81.quote_or_event: “Charity and worship are the primary doties [sic] in religion of a house-holder; without them, one cannot be sravaka (house-holder). Meditation and study of scriptures are the primary duties of a virtuous monk; there can be no monk without them.”
81.explanation: Jainism splits religious life between the renouncing monk and the lay householder. Here giving (dāna) is not an extra for the householder but part of what makes him a lay follower at all.
81.tie_back: Valluvar says the whole household exists in order to cherish guests, and the Jain verse likewise says that without giving one is not a true householder.
81.source: Saman Suttam v. 297 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
81._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam page, including its typo 'doties'. The verse makes giving essential to householding, though it does not speak of guests as specifically as the Kural does.

82.quote_or_event: “How can a householder be not called greedy who does not offer food etc. to an ascetic, who is full of virtues and accepts gift (food) like a honeybee without causing harm to others, when he (the ascetic) visits his home?”
82.explanation: Amṛtacandra counts failing to feed a visiting ascetic as plain greed, and so as a form of himsa (harm). The next verse says that feeding him from the family's own meal loosens greed.
82.tie_back: Like Valluvar, who says no food is worth eating alone while a guest stands outside, Amṛtacandra condemns the householder who keeps his meal while a worthy visitor is at the door.
82.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 173 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 113 on wisdomlib.org
82._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Vijay K. Jain's translation as quoted on wisdomlib, not Ajit Prasada's canonical one. The Jain guest is specifically an ascetic, not any visitor, and the Kural's 'deathless medicine' hyperbole has no counterpart.

83.quote_or_event: “Not saying they have very little, not saying they have not anything, let them ever exercise fruitful charity to all. Like the pitcher of the mendicant who enters the house-door for alms, it will, in due course, gradually become full.”
83.explanation: The Jain-authored Tamil Nālaṭiyār answers the fear that giving drains a household. Regular giving fills up over time, like a mendicant's alms-pitcher filled a little at each door.
83.tie_back: Valluvar promises that daily hospitality never wears a household into ruin, and the Nālaṭiyār makes the same promise with the image of a pitcher that only fills.
83.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 10 'Liberality', st. 9 (= st. 99), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)
83._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text, used because no canonical verse addresses the fear of being impoverished by giving this directly. Verified verbatim on the sacred-texts.com transcription of the Indian Antiquary translation.

84.quote_or_event: “At that moment the gods caused a rain of perfumed water and flowers, and showered down heavenly treasures; they struck the drums, and in the air they praised the gift.”
84.explanation: After the Brahmin household finally feeds the outcaste-born monk Harikeśa with respect, gods shower treasure on the place of the gift. Jain tradition tells of this kind of shower at worthy almsgiving.
84.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Fortune gladly settling in the house of a cheerful host, and the Jain story has wealth literally rain down where a guest is honoured.
84._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. Jainism has no prosperity goddess who rewards hosts as Śrī does in the Kural. The treasure is a sign of merit (puṇya), and the Kural's stress on the host's glad face is missing.

85.quote_or_event: “The husbandmen throw the corn on high ground and on low ground, hoping (for a return). For the like motive give unto me; I may be the field which may produce merit (as the return for your benevolence).”
85.explanation: Speaking for the begging monk Harikeśa, the yaksha describes giving to a worthy guest as sowing seed in a field that yields merit. A few verses earlier he asks that the mendicant receive what is left over.
85.tie_back: Valluvar asks whether a man who feeds his guests first even needs to sow his field, and the Jain verse uses the same farming image: the guest is the field and the gift is the seed.
85._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. The field-and-seed image is a close match, but the Jain verse makes the guest the field, while the Kural suggests that the host's own field needs no sowing.

86.quote_or_event: “To those men the gates of heaven shall never be closed, who with tender hearts and with a mind in accordance with their alms, greatly rejoicing, give even in poverty according to their ability, even as they did in the day of prosperity.”
86.explanation: The Nālaṭiyār promises a heavenly birth to the steady, glad giver who keeps giving even when poor. In Jain terms this reward comes from merit (puṇya), not as a god's gift.
86.tie_back: Valluvar's host, who tends the departing guest and watches for the next, becomes a welcome guest in heaven, and the Nālaṭiyār likewise opens heaven's gates to the habitual, glad-hearted giver.
86.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 10 'Liberality', st. 1 (= st. 91), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)
86._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text, verified verbatim on the sacred-texts.com transcription. It matches the heavenly reward but not the Kural's picture of a host who watches the road for guests or its wordplay of the host becoming a guest.

87.quote_or_event: “The effect of giving of the gift–dāna–has distinctions based on the specific manner in which it is given–vidhiviśeṣa, the specific thing given–dravyaviśeṣa, the specific nature of the giver–dātṛviśeṣa, and the specific nature of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.”
87.explanation: Umāsvāti's sutra says the merit of a gift varies, depending partly on the worth of the person who receives it. Pūjyapāda's commentary compares this to good soil making a seed yield a rich harvest.
87.tie_back: Valluvar says the fruit of the 'sacrifice' of hospitality cannot be fixed in advance but depends on the worth of the guest, which is exactly the Jain teaching of pātraviśeṣa.
87.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
87._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. This is a near one-to-one match for the idea that the fruit is measured by the guest; the sutra adds manner, thing given and giver as further variables.

88.quote_or_event: “He who in this life has done no good actions and has not practised the Law, repents of it in the next world when he has become a prey to Death.”
88.explanation: The monk Citra warns his rich former brother, King Brahmadatta, that wealth and kin are left behind at death and only karma goes with a person. Whoever neglects good deeds will regret it too late.
88.tie_back: Valluvar has hoarders who never took up hospitality lament too late that they have nothing to hold on to, and the Jain sage gives the same warning of a regret that comes only after death.
88._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. It matches the too-late regret, but it speaks of good deeds in general rather than hospitality, and the regret comes in the next birth rather than in this life.

89.quote_or_event: “He who employs not his time in enjoying his property, or gives not of it to ascetics, but lays it up (like a miser)--at him, the foolish one, about to perish, his hoarded wealth shall mock, and the favour of the world shall mock.”
89.explanation: In its chapter on illiberality, the Nālaṭiyār calls the rich man who neither uses nor gives his wealth a fool. His hoard ends up mocking him.
89.tie_back: Valluvar calls poverty in the midst of plenty a folly found only in fools, and the Nālaṭiyār likewise names the wealthy man who will not give 'the foolish one'.
89.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 28 'Illiberality', st. 3 (= st. 273), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)
89._accuracy_note: A Tamil Jain text, used because it matches the Kural's 'folly' framing almost exactly. Verified verbatim on the sacred-texts.com transcription; the recipient is specified as ascetics rather than guests in general.

90.quote_or_event: “And the right manner for giving of gift consists in: respectful welcome, a high seat, washing the feet, worshipping, bowing, purity of mind, speech and body, and purity of food.”
90.explanation: Jain rules for hosting a visiting monk put the manner of welcome first: respectful greeting, a seat, and purity of mind and speech, before the food itself. The Sarvarthasiddhi likewise ranks a gift by whether the guest is received 'with reverence or without reverence'.
90.tie_back: Valluvar says a guest wilts at a face that turns aside even before the meal begins, and Jainism likewise makes the respectful welcome the first and essential part of the gift.
90.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 168 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 113 on wisdomlib.org; cf. Sarvārthasiddhi on Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39
90._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib (Vijay K. Jain's translation, not Ajit Prasada's). It establishes that the manner of welcome comes first, but has nothing like the Kural's anicham-flower image of how quickly a cold look wounds.
